title: Sell Mineral Rights in Big Horn County, WY
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Big Horn County, WY
metaDescription: Own mineral rights in Big Horn County, WY? This is legacy Bighorn Basin oil ground, Elk Basin and Byron fields, split estate, decades of family fractions.
heroLead: Big Horn County sits on some of the oldest producing oil ground in Wyoming, and the courthouse in Basin holds nearly a century of leases, deeds, and probate filings to prove it.
intro: The Bighorn Basin's early oil fields came in fast in the 1910s and 20s, when Elk Basin, Byron, Grass Creek, and Garland turned this stretch of north-central Wyoming into a working oilfield years before most of the rest of the state saw a rig. That early start means Big Horn County carries a longer, more tangled ownership history than newer plays, deeds that reference original homestead patents, probate orders spanning three or four generations, and mineral fractions split so many times that a single quarter section might list a dozen owners.

I've spent enough time in the county recorder's office in Basin to know how to read that history. Most of the calls I get from Big Horn County owners start the same way: someone found an old deed, or a royalty check finally stopped coming, and nobody in the family knows what it means anymore. I can usually tell you within a few days.

sections.heading: The legacy fields that built this county
paragraphs: Elk Basin straddles the Wyoming-Montana line near Deaver and Frannie, and it's been producing since 1915, one of the true old-guard Wyoming oil fields. Byron field, right around the town that shares its name, has similarly deep roots. Both fields have gone through primary production, then secondary waterflood recovery, and in some cases tertiary methods to keep pulling oil from formations that have been worked for over a hundred years.

That longevity is a double-edged sword for mineral owners. On one hand, it means there's real, documented royalty history to price an interest against if your tract sits inside a producing unit. On the other, decline curves on fields this mature are typically gentle but modest, nothing like the steep early production numbers you'd see out of a new horizontal well elsewhere in the state.

Grass Creek and Oregon Basin, technically straddling into neighboring Park County, round out the historic core that put this part of the Bighorn Basin on the map before most other Wyoming plays existed.

sections.heading: Split estate and old homestead patents
paragraphs: Much of Big Horn County was settled under the Homestead Act and later reclamation-era irrigation projects, particularly around the Shoshone and Bighorn River bottomland near Basin, Burlington, Cowley, and Deaver. Many of those original patents included full mineral rights, which families later severed off through lease bonuses or outright sales during exploration booms.

The result today is a lot of split estate: one owner on the surface, farming or ranching the ground, and a different set of owners, often scattered heirs, holding the mineral interest beneath it. Confirming which situation applies to your specific tract is the first thing I do, because it changes both what you own and how a sale would work.

sections.heading: Untangling multi-generation fractions
paragraphs: Because so many Big Horn County mineral interests trace back to homesteads from the 1900s and 1910s, it's common for a single interest to have passed through three, four, or even five rounds of inheritance by now. I've worked files where an eighth-generation fraction of a quarter section is split between a dozen cousins who've never met each other.

That doesn't make the interest impossible to sell, it just means the title work takes patience. I pull the recorder's grantor-grantee index in Basin, trace the probate orders where they exist, and confirm exactly what percentage of what acreage you hold before I ever quote a number. If co-owners want to sell together, I can coordinate that too, but I'll always price your specific fraction on its own merits first.

sections.heading: What actually drives value here
paragraphs: For a producing interest inside an active Elk Basin, Byron, or Grass Creek unit, I look at your trailing royalty statements and the field's current secondary or tertiary recovery status to gauge remaining runway. For undeveloped acreage away from those trends, I price against recent comparable Big Horn County transactions, adjusted for proximity to production.

Either way, I never quote a flat per-acre number without checking your specific tract first. Big Horn County has too much variation, mature waterflood units next to acreage that's never seen a permit, for a one-size number to mean anything honest.

faqs.question: Which towns in Big Horn County have active oil production?
faqs.answer: Byron, Deaver, Cowley, and Burlington all sit near or within legacy field boundaries, with Basin serving as the county seat where the records are filed. I'll check your specific location against current unit maps.

faqs.question: My family's mineral interest has passed through several estates. Where do I start?
faqs.answer: Send me whatever documentation you have, even a single old deed or a probate order name, and I'll trace the rest through the Big Horn County recorder's records.

faqs.question: Is Elk Basin still producing after over a century?
faqs.answer: Portions remain active under secondary recovery. I'll check the current status tied to your specific interest before discussing value.

faqs.question: How is a mature field priced compared to a new play elsewhere in Wyoming?
faqs.answer: Mature fields typically show gentler decline but less speculative upside. I price against actual trailing royalty history rather than assumptions borrowed from newer, unrelated plays.

faqs.question: Do I need to sell my ranch surface along with the minerals?
faqs.answer: No. Split estate is common throughout Big Horn County, and mineral sales are entirely separate from surface ownership, grazing, or farming operations.
